safety_line: Bites are rare and defensive but medically significant — alpha-latrotoxin can cause serious symptoms. See a doctor for a suspected bite, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Glossy jet black body with a red hourglass mark on the underside of the abdomen
Messy, strong, low web in undisturbed corners — garages, meter boxes, woodpiles
Hides by day, hangs upside down at night
Females about 1.25 cm body length, males much smaller and rarely seen

look_alikes.difference: Black widow is glossy black with a red hourglass; brown widow is tan-brown with an orange hourglass and a spiky, sandspur-like egg sac.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the underside of the abdomen and any egg sac.

copy.what_it_means: Bites are rare and almost always defensive — they happen when a hand reaches blind into her hiding spot. This is the one Florida spider worth professional attention when found where kids or pets play.
copy.fact: Bites are rare and defensive — nearly all happen when a hand reaches blind into her hiding spot.
copy.blurb: The one Florida spider worth professional attention when found where kids or pets play.

tech_notes: Confirm red hourglass underside. Deweb + void treatment in undisturbed harborage; advise on clutter/storage reduction.

safety_line: Venom is potent but this species injects less of it and bites less readily than the black widow. See a doctor for a suspected bite, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Tan to brown with an orange hourglass underneath (less bold than the black widow’s red)
Spiky, spherical egg sacs like tiny sea mines — the clearest tell
Web in furniture joints, meter boxes, and pool-cage corners
Tends to curl up rather than attack when disturbed

look_alikes.difference: Brown widow is tan-brown with an orange hourglass and a spiky egg sac; black widow is glossy black with a red hourglass and a smooth egg sac.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the underside of the abdomen and any egg sac.

copy.what_it_means: Now more common than black widows in much of Florida, but notably shyer and less prone to bite. Respect rather than panic — gloves when moving stored patio furniture, and treatment if egg sacs multiply.
copy.fact: Now more common than black widows in much of Florida — but notably shyer and less prone to bite.
copy.blurb: Respect, don’t panic. Gloves when moving stored patio furniture; treat if egg sacs multiply.

tech_notes: Confirm orange hourglass + spiky egg sac. Deweb + void treatment; advise on clutter/storage reduction.

safety_line: Bites only if held or pinched, and feel about like a bee sting. No medical concern for most people.
traits: Large yellow-and-tan spider, females 24-40 mm, in a huge wheel web across paths
Web silk has a golden tint in sunlight
Brown-orange banded legs with tufts of hair on some segments
Sits head-down near the top of the web

look_alikes.difference: Golden silk orb-weaver has banded, tufted legs and a golden web; yellow garden spider has a bold black-and-yellow abdomen and a zigzag web decoration.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the whole web, then zoom in on the leg pattern.

copy.what_it_means: Eats mosquitoes and flies all day and rebuilds damaged sections of its web nightly. Relocate the web if it crosses a walkway; there is no need to kill the spider.
copy.fact: Her silk is, weight for weight, tougher than steel — and she rebuilds damaged sections of the web nightly.
copy.blurb: Eats mosquitoes and flies all day. Relocate the web if it’s across your walkway; don’t kill the engineer.

tech_notes: Beneficial; no treatment. If relocation is requested, move the whole web frame rather than destroying it.

safety_line: Not dangerous to people, though a bite from handling one can be locally painful. No medical concern for most people.
traits: Very large, flat body about 1 inch long with a 3-5 inch leg span
Legs angle forward like a crab, letting it squeeze into narrow gaps
Explosively fast when startled
Tan to brown with a cream marginal band around the carapace

look_alikes.difference: Huntsman spiders are flatter with crab-like forward legs; wolf spiders are stouter, hairier, and their eyes reflect flashlight light distinctly.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the leg posture from above, plus a flashlight eye-shine check at night.

copy.what_it_means: Terrifying-looking and not considered dangerous, but genuinely useful — it actively hunts and eats cockroaches. One on patrol is a roach’s worst night; there is no need to treat for it.
copy.fact: A dedicated cockroach hunter — one huntsman on patrol is a roach’s worst night.
copy.blurb: Terrifying-looking, not considered dangerous, genuinely useful. The scream is optional.

tech_notes: Beneficial predator of roaches; no treatment needed. Relocate outdoors if the customer prefers it gone.

safety_line: Venom is not dangerous to people; a bite from handling one can be locally painful, like a bee sting.
traits: No web — hunts on the ground at speed
Stout, hairy, brown to tan with at least one row of dark stripes from the eyes to the abdomen
Eyeshine sparkles distinctly when scanned with a flashlight at night
Females carry an egg sac, then dozens of spiderlings, on their back

look_alikes.difference: Wolf spiders are stouter and hairier with distinct flashlight eye-shine; huntsman spiders are flatter with crab-like forward-angled legs.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the leg posture from above, plus a flashlight eye-shine check at night.

copy.what_it_means: Mothers carry their spiderlings piggyback — dozens riding along until they can hunt on their own. This is free roach and cricket control; scoop-and-release beats squishing.
copy.fact: Mothers carry their spiderlings piggyback, dozens riding shotgun — one of the few spiders that does this.
copy.blurb: Free roach and cricket control. Scoop-and-release beats squishing.

tech_notes: Beneficial predator; indicates outdoor insect activity nearby. No treatment needed; check door sweeps if found indoors repeatedly.

traits: Small, flat, hard shell-like abdomen shaped like a crab, white or yellow with black spots
Six pointed spines sticking out around the edge of the abdomen
Black legs with small white spots, held out flat rather than curled
Neat, wheel-shaped web strung between shrubs, porch rails or garden edges

look_alikes.difference: Spinybacked orbweaver is tiny with a flat, spiny, disc-shaped body; yellow garden spider is much larger with a smooth, elongated black-and-yellow abdomen
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the abdomen shape — flat and spiny versus large, smooth and black-and-yellow.

safety_line: Its venom is negligible to people; it could in theory bite if handled, but this isn't a spider that bites in practice.

copy.what_it_means: A harmless, oddly spiky little spider that spins a neat web at the edge of the yard and helps clean up flying insects. Its unusual crab-like shape is easy to spot but nothing to worry about.
copy.fact: Those hard spines on its back are thought to make it harder for birds to swallow, an unusual defense for such a small spider.

tech_notes: Harmless web builder; no control action needed unless web placement is a nuisance at an entryway. Per BRIEF Revision 3 rule 5, safety.bites is true as a capability flag (it is not aggressive and essentially never bites people in practice).

review.notes: Per audit item 44: safety.bites changed from false to true (capability, not danger, per rule 5); risk changed from low to defensive to match. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Large spider with a bold black-and-yellow patterned abdomen and a mostly white front section
A dense zigzag band of silk (stabilimentum) running through the center of its web
Big, round web up to about two feet across, usually low in sunny garden edges or against eaves
Sits still in the center of its web most of the day rather than hiding

look_alikes.difference: Yellow garden spider's web has a zigzag band through the center; golden-silk orb-weaver has a long banana-shaped abdomen and a plain web
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the whole web showing whether there is a zigzag pattern through the middle.

safety_line: Bites only if handled and cause no more than brief, mild irritation for most people.

copy.what_it_means: A large, strikingly patterned garden spider that stays put in its web all day and helps control flying pests. It looks intimidating but is not aggressive and is worth leaving in place at the edge of a garden bed.
copy.fact: The zigzag band woven into the center of its web gave it the old nickname 'writing spider,' though no one is fully sure what the band is for.

tech_notes: Beneficial, non-aggressive web builder; no control action needed unless the web itself is a walkway nuisance.

traits: Plump, dull brown to gray spider with a rounded, humped abdomen
Builds a large, complete round web fresh each evening, strung between eaves, trees or porch corners
Web is usually gone by morning, along with the spider, which hides nearby during the day
Most often noticed at night near porch lights, where the web catches flying insects

look_alikes.difference: Tropical orb-weaver hangs still in a large round web it rebuilds each night; huntsman spider has no web and moves fast across walls and ceilings
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph whether the spider is sitting in a web or moving freely on a flat surface.

safety_line: Its venom is negligible to people; it could in theory bite if handled, but this isn't a spider that bites in practice.

copy.what_it_means: A common nighttime spider that builds a fresh web across a porch or between trees every evening and takes it down before morning, catching plenty of flying insects along the way. It is one of the more startling-looking spiders people find lit up near a porch light, and it isn't dangerous.
copy.fact: It tears down and eats its own web most mornings, recycling the silk to build a brand new one the following night.

tech_notes: Harmless nocturnal web builder; rebuilds nightly and is typically gone/hidden by day. No control action needed unless web placement blocks a doorway. Per BRIEF Revision 3 rule 5, safety.bites is true as a capability flag (not aggressive, essentially never bites people in practice).

review.notes: Confirmed against UF/IFAS EDIS IN568 (Featured Creatures: Tropical Orb Weaver Spider): "the web is constructed after dark, and the orb is taken down before dawn," and all stages occur throughout the year in Florida. The source doesn't specifically mention porch lights, but that detail follows from its documented night-flying-insect diet and isn't contradicted. Per audit item 44: safety.bites changed from false to true (capability, not danger, per rule 5); risk changed from low to defensive to match; copy's 'harmless' softened since bites is now true. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Small, slender, elongated abdomen, silvery-white with dark lines down the back and reddish-orange marks underneath
Legs are long, thin and green to greenish-black with darker bands at the joints
Web is held nearly flat and tilted, unlike most orb webs which hang straight up and down
Usually found low in shaded shrubs, under tree branches or along garden edges rather than in open sun

look_alikes.difference: Orchard orb-weaver spins a neat, flat, tilted web and has silvery-green markings; cellar spider is plain pale gray with a messy, shapeless web
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the whole web showing whether it is a neat round shape or a tangled mess.

safety_line: Its venom is negligible to people; it could in theory bite if handled, but this isn't a spider that bites in practice.

copy.what_it_means: A small, delicate spider that builds a neatly tilted web low in shady shrubs and helps keep flying insect numbers down. It is not aggressive and isn't dangerous, and rarely comes to anyone's attention beyond its unusual sideways-tilted web.
copy.fact: Unlike most orb-weavers, it holds its web nearly flat and at an angle instead of straight up and down, which is an easy way to recognize its web even before spotting the spider.

tech_notes: Non-aggressive web builder; no control action needed. Per BRIEF Revision 3 rule 5, safety.bites is true as a capability flag (not aggressive, essentially never bites people in practice).

review.notes: Source corrected to UF/IFAS EDIS IN1243, which is specifically about Leucauge argyrobapta (and the near-identical L. venusta) and confirms silvery-white abdomen with dark lines and reddish-orange ventral marks, green/greenish-black legs banded at the joints, and a mostly horizontal (under 45 degrees) web. It also distinguishes the truly different L. argyra (dorsal lines that turn inward 90 degrees, no reddish-orange spots), so traits are now correctly matched to this species rather than argyra. Per audit item 44: safety.bites changed from false to true (capability, not danger, per rule 5); risk changed from low to defensive to match; copy's 'harmless' softened since bites is now true. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Bright green body with fine black spines and specks, blending in with leaves and stems
A reddish patch and a few red spots between the eyes
No web; sits still on flowers and shrubs, then pounces on passing insects
Females guard a round, spiky egg sac on a plant stem and defend it aggressively if disturbed

look_alikes.difference: Green lynx spider is bright green with black spines and pounces cat-like from a leaf; crab spider sits still and moves sideways like a crab
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the front legs and body shape while the spider is on the plant.

safety_line: Rarely bites unless handled or its egg sac is disturbed; the bite is painful but not dangerous, with swelling that fades after a day or two.

copy.what_it_means: A bright green, plant-dwelling spider that hunts by ambush instead of building a web and helps keep garden pest insects in check. It is not aggressive toward people unless it is picked up or its egg sac is disturbed, so it is best left alone on the plant.
copy.fact: It hunts like a cat stalking prey, pouncing on insects from a still position on a leaf rather than trapping them in silk.

tech_notes: Beneficial ambush predator on garden plants; avoid handling, especially near an egg sac, but no control action is needed.

traits: Large, fuzzy spider with big, forward-facing eyes and an alert, curious posture
Iridescent green or blue fangs (chelicerae) that can flash in the light
Males are black with bold white markings; females come in shades of orange, tan, brown or gray
Moves in short, sudden hops instead of running or spinning a web to catch prey

look_alikes.difference: Jumping spider has large forward-facing eyes and hops, often 'looking' at the camera; wolf spider has smaller eyes and just runs fast
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in straight-on at the face showing eye size and arrangement.

safety_line: Bites only if handled roughly, and reactions are usually mild and short-lived for most people.

copy.what_it_means: The largest jumping spider in the eastern US, a harmless, curious hunter that stalks and pounces on insects instead of building a web. Many people find it endearing once they notice it seems to watch them back.
copy.fact: It has some of the sharpest vision of any spider, which is why it often turns to track a person's movement instead of fleeing.

tech_notes: Harmless, non-aggressive hunting spider; beneficial insect predator. No control action needed.

traits: Females are dark brown to black, compact, and stay hidden in a crack or crevice with a small tangled web around the entrance
Males are tan to gray-brown with unusually long, thin legs and are the ones people find wandering indoors
No violin-shaped marking on the head, unlike a brown recluse
Web looks like fine, velcro-like fuzz around a gap in siding, brick or a window frame rather than a neat wheel shape

look_alikes.difference: House spider males have very long thin legs and no head marking; brown recluse (rare in Florida) has a violin-shaped mark on the head
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the top of the head/body showing whether a violin-shaped marking is present.

safety_line: Not considered medically dangerous, but it can bite if handled. Leave it undisturbed rather than picking it up.

copy.what_it_means: One of the most commonly misidentified spiders in Florida: wandering males are often mistaken for brown recluse spiders, which aren't established here. It can bite if handled, but it isn't considered medically dangerous — better left undisturbed than picked up.
copy.fact: Its long-legged wandering males are the ones usually found indoors and mistaken for a brown recluse, even though checking for a violin mark tells them apart.

tech_notes: Frequent 'brown recluse' misidentification; confirm absence of violin marking and note that L. reclusa is not established in Florida. Not considered medically dangerous; can bite if handled — advise leaving it undisturbed rather than handling. No control action needed beyond routine perimeter service if client wants fewer web sites.

review.notes: Corrected per outside review: UF/IFAS reports bite cases for this species; bites is now true and copy no longer claims it can't break skin. Per audit item 49: tech_notes cited 'P. brunnea' alongside L. reclusa as if both were the recluse's scientific name; P. brunnea (Periplaneta brunnea) is actually the brown cockroach, unrelated to spiders -- removed the erroneous reference. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Plain tan to dark brown spider with a darker violin-shaped marking on the head/shoulder area
Six eyes arranged in three pairs rather than the eight eyes most spiders have
Legs are plain, with no spines, bands or bright markings
Body about 1/4 to 3/8 inch long (about quarter-sized with legs spread), with legs attached close to the body

look_alikes.difference: Wandering male southern house spiders are the most common recluse look-alike in Florida, with much longer thin legs and no violin marking on the head
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo can't confirm a brown recluse; the eye pattern needs magnification. From a safe distance, never handle it; a technician can confirm on site.

look_alikes.difference: Yellow sac spider is smaller, pale yellow-beige with darker leg tips and no violin marking; a genuine brown recluse has a distinct dark violin shape on the head
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo can't confirm a brown recluse; the eye pattern needs magnification. From a safe distance, never handle it; a technician can confirm on site.

safety_line: A confirmed bite can occasionally cause a slow-healing wound; see a doctor if a bite site worsens, blisters or does not start healing within a few days.

copy.what_it_means: A spider that is not actually established in Florida outside rare, isolated cases, even though its name gets used constantly for skin wounds of unknown cause. A clear photo of the violin marking suggests the ID, but doesn't prove it — most turn out to be a harmless local spider once confirmed.
copy.fact: It has six eyes arranged in three pairs instead of the eight most spiders have, which is one of the most reliable ways experts confirm the species under magnification.

tech_notes: Not established in Florida; isolated indoor populations have occasionally turned up but do not spread. Most submitted 'recluse' photos in FL are Kukulcania hibernalis males or other species; confirm violin marking and 6-eye arrangement before treating as a confirmed ID. Medical dermonecrotic wounds are frequently misattributed to this species (often actually MRSA or other causes) -- do not diagnose, refer to a doctor.

review.notes: Verdict/urgency are a deliberate judgment call: kept at watch/moderate rather than call/high specifically because the species is not established in Florida, to avoid fear-marketing a spider that is very unlikely to be the true culprit; owner should confirm this framing is what they want for this entry. Per audit item 46: traits[3] previously stated the Florida non-establishment fact, which isn't a visible trait; replaced with a size feature. The non-establishment fact is still covered in copy.what_it_means and tech_notes. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Small, pale yellow-beige spider with noticeably darker tips on the legs and jaws
A faint orange-brown stripe often runs down the center of the back
Builds a small, flat silk sac tucked into a ceiling-wall corner or under furniture to hide in during the day
Hunts actively at night rather than sitting in a web

look_alikes.difference: Yellow sac spider is pale yellow-beige with dark leg tips; a genuine brown recluse is duller brown with a dark violin mark on the head
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the top of the head/body showing overall color and whether a violin-shaped marking is present.

safety_line: The most common indoor spider bite in many homes; usually mild pain and itching that clears up in about a week. See a doctor if a bite site worsens or does not improve.

copy.what_it_means: One of the most common spiders to actually bite people indoors, usually while wandering at night or hiding in a small silk sac tucked in a corner or under clutter. Bites are painful but generally minor and heal within about a week, and routine indoor treatment helps reduce numbers.
copy.fact: It is often unfairly blamed for wounds actually caused by a brown recluse, even though its own bite is far more common and generally much milder.

tech_notes: Frequently the true culprit behind bites blamed on brown recluse in areas where the recluse is not established. Locate/remove silk sacs in corners; treat per label for indoor populations.

traits: Small, pale grayish body with extremely long, thin, delicate legs
Loose, messy, irregular web strung in a high corner, garage or closet rather than a neat wheel shape
Hangs upside down in the web and vibrates rapidly when disturbed
Often confused with the non-spider daddy longlegs (harvestman), which has no web and a single oval body

look_alikes.difference: Cellar spider has a small two-part body, long legs and sits in a messy web; harvestman has one fused oval body, no web, and just walks
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph whether the body looks like one oval blob or two separate parts, and whether there is a web.

safety_line: Its venom is not considered medically significant, and it very rarely bites people even if picked up.

copy.what_it_means: A harmless, gentle spider often called a daddy long legs, at the center of an old myth that it's the world's most venomous spider with fangs too weak to break skin. Neither part holds up — its venom isn't medically significant, and it can bite on the rare occasion it's handled, with no real effect.
copy.fact: Testing has shown its venom is nowhere near strong enough to be dangerous, putting the old 'world's most venomous spider' myth firmly to rest.

tech_notes: Harmless and beneficial (preys on other spiders/insects); commonly confused with harvestman. No control action needed beyond routine web removal for tidiness.

review.notes: safety.bites changed to true to match the copy's own admission that it rarely bites — an earlier draft said both 'cannot bite' and 'does bite on rare occasion' in the same entry. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Front two pairs of legs are noticeably longer and held out to the sides, crab-like
Moves sideways and backward as easily as forward, unlike most spiders
Colors range from white, pink and yellow to green or brown, and some species slowly shift color to match the flower they sit on
No web; sits motionless on a flower or leaf waiting to ambush visiting insects

look_alikes.difference: Crab spider sits still on a flower, sometimes matching its color, and moves sideways; green lynx spider is bright green and pounces actively
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the front legs and body shape while the spider is on the plant.

safety_line: Its venom is negligible to people; it could in theory bite if handled, but it is not aggressive and this isn't a spider that bites in practice.

copy.what_it_means: A little ambush hunter that sits still on flowers waiting for pollinators and other insects to come within reach. It is not known to be harmful to people and is a normal part of a healthy garden.
copy.fact: Some species can slowly change color over several days to blend in with the exact flower they are hunting from.

tech_notes: Non-aggressive garden predator; no control action needed. Per BRIEF Revision 3 rule 5, safety.bites is true as a capability flag (not aggressive, essentially never bites people in practice).

review.notes: Per audit item 44: safety.bites changed from false to true (capability, not danger, per rule 5); risk changed from low to defensive to match. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.
